guest_hosts.credential_frame: A composite of engineers who have worked on catheter-based fetal intervention tools — shunt delivery systems, intrauterine access devices — navigating FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption pathways and the specific mechanical constraints of operating through a pregnant uterus
guest_hosts.delivery_baseline: Measured pace, slightly clipped consonants, answers questions one layer deeper than asked — not to show off but because the surface answer is genuinely incomplete
guest_hosts.expertise: Why instrument design choices in fetal surgery are not just miniaturization problems — they are simultaneous mechanical, materials, and regulatory constraint problems. Can explain concretely why the Somatex parasol geometry solved a dislocation problem the Harrison cannula couldn't, why membrane sealing after instrument withdrawal is a materials science dead end at current scales, and why a gene therapy delivery device is a categorically different regulatory object than a shunt or a laser fiber.
guest_hosts.field: minimally invasive surgical device engineering, with a focus on obstetric and neonatal applications
guest_hosts.label: MAREN
guest_hosts.personality: Precise and slightly impatient with abstraction — will interrupt a vague claim to ask what gauge, what material, what failure mode. Not unkind, but has a low tolerance for engineering elegance being mistaken for clinical readiness. Occasionally dry about the gap between what a prototype can do in a lab and what a scrub tech can set up at 2am.
guest_hosts.role_in_episode: Enters after the shunt comparison beat to explain why the Somatex result is not just a better design story but a regulatory and manufacturing story. Stays through the PPROM beat to explain why it resists instrumentation solutions. Provides the sharpest pushback on robotic hype — not from clinical evidence but from the manufacturing and sterilization realities that precede clinical trials. Exits before the gene therapy beat so Juno and Caspar can close on the open frontier without an engineer's voice narrowing the frame.

key_claims.claim: NAFTNet has grown from 18 centers at founding to 57 leading medical centers across the US, Canada, Mexico, and South America as of 2026.
The TOTAL trial showed FETO improved survival to discharge from 15% to 40% in severe left-sided CDH, but increased risk of preterm prelabor rupture of membranes.
Karl Storz fetoscopes remain the only FDA-approved fetoscopy instruments for TTTS, creating a near-monopoly in the US market.

The Somatex intrauterine shunt showed significantly better outcomes than the Harrison shunt for LUTO (84.8% vs 50% live birth rate), attributed to its smaller 18G delivery cannula and self-deploying parasol design.
Robotic-assisted fetal surgery is currently in experimental stage but expected to play a decisive role in the future, with KU Leuven and other groups developing flexible robotic endoscopes.

The MOMS trial (published 2011) established that prenatal spina bifida repair reduces need for VP shunting and improves motor outcomes at 30 months, but with maternal/fetal risks including ~46% PPROM rate.
First-in-human fetal gene therapy trials are now being designed, with GM1 gangliosidosis as an initial target (Tippi MacKenzie, UCSF).
PPROM remains the Achilles heel of fetal intervention, complicating 30-40% of preterm deliveries and occurring in 32-46% of fetal surgery cases depending on procedure type.
